pos: n. (the son of Seth and grandson of Adam, in whose days men began to call upon the name of the LORD; written Enosh in the Chronicles)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Enosh, man — and specifically man in his frailty and mortality, from a root meaning to be weak or incurable, as distinguished from 'adam, man from the ground, and 'ish, man as male. Luke gives the Greek form Enos in the genealogy of our Lord.
biblical_def: Enos is the third man in the line of promise, and his birth carries one of the most weighted notices in Genesis: “And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD” (Gen 4:26). The verse stands at the end of the chapter that has just traced the line of Cain through city-building, polygamy and Lamech's boast of murder. Against that, one sentence: men began to call upon the name of the LORD. Whether the phrase marks the beginning of public, corporate worship or the beginning of men being called by the name of the LORD, the point is the same — in the generation of the man whose name means frail mortal, the true religion appears in the earth as a visible thing. His life is then given in the register: “And Enos lived ninety years, and begat Cainan” (Gen 5:9), and “And all the days of Enos were nine hundred and five years: and he died” (Gen 5:11). Luke sets him in the descent of Christ: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luk 3:38). Nine hundred and five years, one recorded sentence about his generation, and a place in the line that ends at Bethlehem.

webster_full: ENOS, n. Man, mortal man; the son of Seth and grandson of Adam.

In his days men began to call upon the name of the LORD.
He lived ninety years and begat Cainan, and all his days were nine hundred and five years.
He stands third in the genealogy of our Saviour as it is reckoned by Luke.

And Enos lived ninety years, and begat Cainan:
And all the days of Enos were nine hundred and five years: and he died.
Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God.
corruption_summary: The rise of religion in Genesis 4:26 is commonly explained as the natural evolution of primitive man's response to nature. Scripture presents worship as the response of a people to a God who has already spoken and already promised a Seed.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard account of religion's origin runs from animism through polytheism to monotheism, with Israel's faith a late refinement of a long human development. Genesis reverses the sequence completely. God walks with man in the garden; man falls; God gives the promise of the Seed and clothes the guilty with skins, which required a death; Abel brings a firstling of his flock and is accepted, Cain brings the fruit of the ground and is not; and then, in the days of Enos, calling on the name of the LORD becomes a public practice. Worship in Scripture is never man's upward guess. It is the response of sinners to a revelation and a promise already given.

The name matters to the point. Enosh is man as feeble, mortal, incurable — the word the Psalms use when they ask, “What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?” (Psa 8:4). It was in the generation of frail man that men began to call upon the LORD, and that order is the gospel in miniature: the creature calls because he knows what he is and knows Who has spoken. Paul quotes the promise that runs from this point to the end: “whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Rom 10:13).

pos: n. (the son of Enos and fourth in the line from Adam; written Kenan in the Chronicles, and the name also of a second man in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: From Hebrew Qeynan, connected with qanah, to acquire or possess, and with the same root that gives Cain — hence possession or acquired. Luke gives it as Cainan twice: once for this man, and once in the postdiluvian line between Arphaxad and Sala.
biblical_def: Cainan is the fourth man in the genealogy of Genesis 5, and his entry is one of the plainest in that chapter: “And Enos lived ninety years, and begat Cainan” (Gen 5:9); “And Cainan lived seventy years, and begat Mahalaleel” (Gen 5:12); “And all the days of Cainan were nine hundred and ten years: and he died” (Gen 5:14). The Chronicler opens his history with the same names compressed to a bare list: “Adam, Sheth, Enosh” (1Ch 1:1) and so on through the line. Luke reaches Cainan on his way back to Adam: “Which was the son of Mathusala, which was the son of Enoch, which was the son of Jared, which was the son of Maleleel, which was the son of Cainan” (Luk 3:37). Nothing at all is told of the man himself — no deed, no word, no failing, no virtue. What Genesis 5 supplies instead is a rhythm: he lived, he begat, all his days were so many, and he died. Eight times in the chapter the refrain and he died falls, and it falls on Cainan too. The chapter is the death certificate of a race under sentence, punctuated by the one man of whom it is not said — Enoch, who walked with God, and was not, for God took him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Cainan; in sacred history he is the son of Enos, fourth in descent from Adam, called Kenan in the Chronicles.
webster_full: CAINAN, n. Possession; the son of Enos and the father of Mahalaleel.

A second Cainan is named by Luke, between Arphaxad and Sala, in the generations after the flood.

corruption_summary: The long lives of Genesis 5 are treated as symbolic numerology or as borrowed from Mesopotamian king-lists. The dictionary reads them as the record says: real men, real years, and a chapter written to teach that death reigns.
corruption_paragraphs: The nine-hundred-year lifespans are handled by most modern commentary in one of two ways: as symbolic figures encoding something else, or as a Hebrew imitation of the antediluvian king-lists of Sumer, whose reigns run to tens of thousands of years. The second point actually cuts the other way. Genesis 5 is sober precisely where the pagan lists are extravagant; it gives ordinary numbers in an ordinary style, with fathers begetting at reasonable ages and lifespans that shorten steadily after the flood until they reach the seventy years of Psalm 90. That is not the shape of legend borrowed; it is the shape of a record kept.

More importantly, the chapter has a doctrine in it, and the doctrine is destroyed by allegorising the numbers. Eight times the refrain and he died closes an entry, and Paul states the reason: “Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression” (Rom 5:14). Genesis 5 is a chapter about a sentence being carried out, generation upon generation, no matter how long a man lasted — and about the single exception, Enoch, who did not die because God took him, which is the first hint in Scripture that the sentence is not the last word.

pos: n. (the son of Cainan and fifth in the line from Adam, whose name means the praise of God; called Maleleel by Luke)
etymology: From Hebrew Mahalal'el, from mahalal, praise, and El, God — praise of God, or he that praises God. Luke's Greek gives Maleleel. A later Mahalaleel of the tribe of Judah is named among the dwellers in Jerusalem after the captivity (Neh 11:4).
biblical_def: Mahalaleel is the fifth link in the chain from Adam to Noah, and the record of him is three verses long: “And Cainan lived seventy years, and begat Mahalaleel” (Gen 5:12); “And Mahalaleel lived sixty and five years, and begat Jared” (Gen 5:15); “And all the days of Mahalaleel were eight hundred ninety and five years: and he died” (Gen 5:17). Luke names him in the ascent to Adam as Maleleel (Luk 3:37). What the entry is worth attending to is the name, because the names of Genesis 5 read as a confession when they are laid end to end. Seth, appointed; Enos, frail man; Cainan, possession; Mahalaleel, the praise of God; Jared, descent; Enoch, dedicated; Methuselah; Lamech; Noah, rest. In the very generations under the sentence of death, a father named his son the praise of God. Nothing whatever is recorded of the man's deeds. What is recorded is what a family in the line of promise called their children while the world of Cain was building cities and singing Lamech's song of vengeance.

In Luke's genealogy the Greek form Maleleel is used.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that naming is confession, and that parents in the covenant line have always spoken their theology over their children before those children could speak at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Mahalaleel is a patriarch in a register and nobody has contested him. What his name sets against the modern practice is the seriousness with which Scripture treats naming. In the line of Seth the names carry God in them — Mahalal-el, praise of God — while in the parallel line of Cain the names carry the man: a city named after a son, a boast named after a father. Genesis puts the two registers side by side in chapters 4 and 5 and lets the reader hear the difference in what each family thought worth saying.

The principle to recover is that a household's speech forms its children long before its arguments do. The covenant instruction of Deuteronomy assumes exactly this: the words are to be in the heart, taught diligently, talked of when thou sittest in thine house and when thou walkest by the way (Deu 6:6-7). Paul commands fathers to bring them up “in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4). A man who called his son the praise of God in the eight hundredth year of a dying world was doing what Christian fathers still do at a font and a supper table: saying out loud, over a child who cannot yet answer, whose the house is.

pos: n. (the son of Mahalaleel and father of Enoch, sixth in the line from Adam, whose life was the longest but one before the flood)
etymology: From Hebrew Yered, from yarad, to go down or descend — hence descent. Luke keeps the form Jared. A man of the same name is listed among the sons of Ezra in the tribe of Judah (1Ch 4:18).
biblical_def: Jared lived nine hundred sixty and two years, longer than any man in Scripture except his own grandson Methuselah, and his single distinction in the record is his son. “And Jared lived an hundred sixty and two years, and he begat Enoch” (Gen 5:18); “And all the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty and two years: and he died” (Gen 5:20). The chapter is otherwise a monotony of the same three clauses, and it is broken exactly once, in the entry immediately after Jared's: “And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him” (Gen 5:24). The father of that son gets no such notice, and Scripture never tells us what he was. But the two facts sit next to each other — nine hundred and sixty-two ordinary years, and a son who walked with God and did not see death — and the New Testament twice reaches back past Jared to the son: Hebrews for the faith that pleased God (Heb 11:5), Jude for a prophecy delivered before the flood, “And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints” (Jud 14). Jared is the sixth from Adam; the seventh walked with God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Jared; in sacred history he is the son of Mahalaleel and the father of Enoch, sixth in descent from Adam.
webster_full: JARED, n. Descent; the son of Mahalaleel and the father of Enoch.

All the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty and two years, and he died.
Only Methuselah his grandson is recorded to have lived longer.

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that a godly son is God's gift and not a father's achievement, and that Scripture withholds the credit as deliberately as it records the fact.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jared is a patriarch of the register and nobody has contested him. What his entry sets against the modern reader — particularly the Christian parent — is a striking silence. The most remarkable man before the flood was Enoch, and Scripture says nothing whatever about the household he came out of. It does not credit Jared with his son's walk, and it does not blame him for anything either. The nine hundred sixty-two years are recorded and then the chapter moves on.

The principle to recover is that grace is not hereditary and not manufactured. The covenant promises are to believers and their children and are to be pleaded, and God has ordinarily used faithful homes — but the new birth is His, “Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13). Fathers may teach, discipline, catechise and pray, and must; they cannot regenerate. Jared had one son who walked with God and other sons and daughters of whom nothing is said, and the same house produced both. That is a comfort to grieving parents and a warning to confident ones.

pos: n. (the son of Arphaxad and father of Eber in the line from Shem to Abraham; written Shelah in the Chronicles and Sala by Luke)
etymology: From Hebrew Shelach, generally rendered a sending forth or a sprout, a shoot, from shalach, to send. The Authorized Version writes him Salah in Genesis and Shelah in 1 Chronicles 1:18; Luke gives the Greek Sala. He is a different man altogether from Shelah the third son of Judah, who has his own entry in this dictionary.
biblical_def: Salah stands third in the postdiluvian line, between Arphaxad and Eber: “And Arphaxad begat Salah; and Salah begat Eber” (Gen 10:24), with the dates supplied in the register of Genesis 11: “And Arphaxad lived five and thirty years, and begat Salah” (Gen 11:12), and “And Salah lived thirty years, and begat Eber” (Gen 11:14), living four hundred and three years afterward. The Chronicler spells him Shelah in the compressed roll: “Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah” (1Ch 1:24). His importance lies wholly in the son. Eber is the man from whom the name Hebrew is generally traced, and Genesis marks him out specially: Shem is called “the father of all the children of Eber” (Gen 10:21), and it was in the days of Eber's son Peleg that the earth was divided. So Salah sits at the narrowing of the line: from all mankind after the flood, to Shem, to Arphaxad, to Salah, to Eber, and on down through Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor and Terah to Abram — the funnel by which the promise made to the woman's seed is brought to one household in Mesopotamia. Luke walks the same names backward: “which was the son of Heber, which was the son of Sala” (Luk 3:35).

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that God narrows the line of promise deliberately, name by name, and that election is visible in Scripture as a family tree long before it is stated as a doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Salah is a name in the register and nobody has contested him. What the postdiluvian genealogy sets before the reader is a narrowing. Genesis 10 spreads out into seventy nations, the whole earth peopled from three sons; Genesis 11 then takes one of those sons and follows a single thread through nine generations to one man in Ur. The Bible is the story of that thread. It does not lose interest in the nations — the promise to Abram is that in him all families of the earth shall be blessed — but the route to the many runs through the one.

The principle to recover is that election is not an abstraction bolted onto the gospel by later theologians; it is the shape of the narrative from Genesis 4 onward. Abel not Cain, Seth not the line of Lamech, Shem not Ham, Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau, Judah not Reuben. Paul draws the conclusion from exactly this material: “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16). A reader who finds the doctrine strange has not yet noticed how the genealogies are built.

pos: n. (the son of Peleg and father of Serug, sixth in the postdiluvian line from Shem; called Ragau by Luke)
etymology: From Hebrew Re'u, from ra'ah, a friend or companion, or from ro'eh, a shepherd — hence friend. Luke's Greek gives Ragau. The element appears again in Reuel, friend of God.
biblical_def: Reu is one of the four names — Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah — that carry the line of Shem from Peleg down to Abram, and his entry in the register is the standard form: “And Peleg lived thirty years, and begat Reu” (Gen 11:18); “And Reu lived two and thirty years, and begat Serug” (Gen 11:20); “And Reu lived after he begat Serug two hundred and seven years, and begat sons and daughters” (Gen 11:21). Luke has him as “the son of Ragau, which was the son of Phalec” (Luk 3:35). His life falls in the shadow of two things Genesis has just recorded: the dividing of the earth in the days of his father Peleg, and the tower of Babel with the confounding of the one language. This is the generation in which the nations went their several ways with their several gods, and the register plainly says what became of the line itself. Joshua tells Israel what their fathers were in those centuries: “Your fathers dwelt on the other side of the flood in old time, even Terah, the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor: and they served other gods” (Jos 24:2). Reu's house was drifting into idolatry generation by generation, and the calling of Abram out of it is therefore not the flowering of a family tradition but a rescue.

corruption_summary: The line from Shem to Abraham is often read as the pedigree of a family that kept the true religion alive. Joshua says the opposite — they served other gods — and the doctrine of grace depends on hearing him.
corruption_paragraphs: It is natural, and wrong, to assume that the men listed between Shem and Abram were a faithful remnant handing down the worship of the true God through the centuries after Babel. Scripture does not say so of any of them, and it says the reverse of the household at the end of the list. Joshua stands the whole nation before the LORD at Shechem and begins his covenant address by telling them their ancestors were idolaters. Terah served other gods; Abram was taken from among them. Whatever knowledge of God survived in that house, it did not save it.

The doctrine is total depravity and sovereign grace, stated as family history rather than as a proposition. Man left to himself does not preserve the truth; he trades it, as Paul says, changing “the truth of God into a lie” (Rom 1:25) and worshipping the creature. The line from Reu to Terah is not a chain of faithful men keeping a lamp lit; it is a lineage sliding into the same darkness as the nations, out of which God reached and called one man. Every genuine conversion since has the same structure, and every family that has been in the church three generations should read Joshua 24:2 with attention.

pos: n. (the son of Reu and grandfather of Terah, seventh in the postdiluvian line from Shem; called Saruch by Luke)
etymology: From Hebrew Serug, from a root meaning to intertwine, interlace or entwine — hence branch or tendril. Luke gives the Greek Saruch. The name survives as that of a town in northern Mesopotamia near Haran, in the very district where his descendants settled.
biblical_def: Serug is the great-grandfather of Abram, and the record of him is two verses: “And Reu lived two and thirty years, and begat Serug” (Gen 11:20); “And Serug lived thirty years, and begat Nahor” (Gen 11:22); and he lived after that two hundred years, begetting sons and daughters (Gen 11:23). Luke names him Saruch in the descent of Christ (Luk 3:35). What is worth noticing in his generation is the arithmetic of the register: the lifespans are collapsing. Before the flood men lived nine hundred years; Arphaxad, born two years after it, lived four hundred and thirty-eight; Peleg two hundred and thirty-nine; Serug two hundred and thirty; and by Moses' own psalm the span is “threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years” (Psa 90:10). The curse is tightening across the chapter, quietly, in the numbers. Serug's grandson Terah would settle in Haran with his household and their gods; his great-grandson would be called out of it. The name that means a tendril or a branch belongs, in the providence of God, to a link in the line that ends with the Branch: “there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isa 11:1).

corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that the shortening of human life through Genesis 11 is the curse working itself out in plain arithmetic, and that the register is preaching while it counts.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Serug is a name in the register and nobody has contested him. What his generation sets before the attentive reader is a graph. The numbers of Genesis 11 fall away steadily from four hundred and thirty-eight to two hundred and thirty-nine to two hundred and thirty and downward, and no comment is made on the decline at all. Moses simply records it, and then, in the psalm that bears his name, states the figure the race finally settles at. A register that was invented to glorify the ancestors would not have written its own diminishment into the arithmetic.

The principle to recover is that the curse pronounced in Eden is a working reality and not a symbol. “for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19) is being executed in these columns of figures. Paul names the mechanism — “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned” (Rom 5:12) — and the same apostle names the reversal, that the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death. The chapter that counts Serug's two hundred and thirty years is quietly making the case that man cannot outlast his own sentence, and it ends by calling one man out of Ur.

pos: n. (the son of Enoch and grandson of Cain, second in the line of Cain recorded in Genesis)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Iyrad, of uncertain sense; connected by some with 'ir, a city, and by others with a root meaning fugitive or wild ass. He is named once, in the compressed genealogy of Cain's house.
biblical_def: Irad belongs to the shorter and darker of the two genealogies in Genesis. After Cain went out from the presence of the LORD and dwelt in the land of Nod, he built a city and named it after his son Enoch — not the Enoch who walked with God, who belongs to the other line entirely. The register then runs in a single verse: “And unto Enoch was born Irad: and Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech” (Gen 4:18). Four generations in twenty-six words, and then the narrative stops on Lamech, who took two wives and made the first recorded song in Scripture a boast of killing: “I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt” (Gen 4:23), and “If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold” (Gen 4:24). The line is not without gifts — from it came the fathers of herdsmen, of musicians, and of workers in brass and iron. Moses is not describing barbarians. He is describing culture without God: cities, arts, metallurgy, poetry, and a man who could turn a marriage into an audience for his revenge. Irad is the second name in that descent, and Scripture tells us nothing of him but the name and the place he holds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Irad; in sacred history he is the son of Enoch the son of Cain, in the line of Cain before the flood.
webster_full: IRAD, n. A proper name in the fourth chapter of Genesis.
The son of Enoch, and the grandson of Cain.
He is the second in the genealogy of the house of Cain.
He begat Mehujael, and from Mehujael descended Methusael and Lamech.
Of his life and deeds the Scripture records nothing whatever.

And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt. I
corruption_summary: Genesis 4 is read today as a myth about the invention of civilisation. Moses writes it as history, and as the account of a culture of real achievement raised by men in flight from God.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is commonly classed with the culture-hero myths of the ancient near east: a tale explaining how men came to keep cattle, make music and work metal. But Moses is doing something a myth never does — he is passing a moral verdict on the achievements he records. The tents, the harp and organ, the artificer in brass and iron are all named without a sneer; these are genuine goods, and the Bible does not despise them. What the chapter sets against them is the trajectory of the house that produced them: out from the presence of the LORD, into a city named for a man, into polygamy, and into a song celebrating a killing.

The principle is common grace and its limits. God gives real ability to men who hate Him, and the arts and sciences of the unbelieving world are His gifts, not the devil's inventions. Calvin insisted on this from these very verses. But talent is not righteousness, and a civilisation may be brilliant and damned at once. Genesis 6 gives the summary of what the two lines had come to: “GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Gen 6:5). Irad is one silent name inside that verdict.

pos: n. (the son of Irad and father of Methusael, third in the line of Cain)
etymology: From Hebrew Mechuya'el, most naturally read as smitten of God, from machah, to blot out or smite, with El, God. It is a striking name to find in the house of Cain, where the divine element is otherwise absent, and the sense it carries is judgment rather than praise.
biblical_def: Mehujael is the third name in the line of Cain, and like the others in that list he appears in one verse and never again: “And unto Enoch was born Irad: and Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech” (Gen 4:18). The two genealogies of Genesis 4 and 5 are laid side by side on purpose, and they are meant to be compared. In the line of Seth the names confess God as praise, dedication and rest — Mahalaleel, the praise of God; Enoch, dedicated; Noah, rest. In the line of Cain the one name that carries El at all appears to mean smitten of God. Whether the father meant it as lament, as defiance, or as a plain description of a family under a mark, Scripture does not say. What Scripture does record of the house is its trajectory: a city, two wives taken by one man, a boast of blood, and then the flood. The chapter ends by turning back to the other line and to Enos, in whose days men began to call on the name of the LORD — the deliberate contrast on which the whole of Genesis 4 closes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Mehujael; in sacred history he is the son of Irad, in the genealogy of the house of Cain.
webster_full: MEHUJAEL, n. Smitten of God; a proper name in the fourth chapter of Genesis.
The son of Irad and the grandson of Enoch, the son of Cain.
He is the third in the line of Cain as it is there recorded.
He begat Methusael, who was the father of Lamech.
Nothing is written of his life beyond his place in the genealogy.

And Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle.
And Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubalcain was Naamah.
And to Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enos: then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that Genesis sets two families side by side and asks the reader to notice which one calls on the name of the LORD, because that division runs through history to this day.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Mehujael is a name in Cain's register and nobody has contested him. What the two genealogies set against the modern reader is the oldest division there is. Augustine built the City of God on it: two cities founded by two loves, one by the love of self to the contempt of God, the other by the love of God to the contempt of self, running through all of history intermingled and separated only at the end. Genesis 4 and 5 are where he found it — one line building a city and singing about revenge, the other calling on the name of the LORD and burying its dead.

The principle to recover is that this division is not between the religious and the irreligious, nor between the cultured and the crude. The line of Cain gave the world music and metallurgy; the line of Seth gave it a list of funerals and one man who walked with God. The distinction is the one Christ draws between two builders whose houses look identical until the rain descends, and the one Paul draws between the natural man who receives not the things of the Spirit of God and the man taught by the Spirit. “But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him” (1Co 2:14).

pos: n. (the son of Mehujael and the father of Lamech, fourth in the line of Cain; not to be confounded with Methuselah in the line of Seth)
etymology: From Hebrew Methusha'el, commonly explained as man of God or who is of God, from math, a man, with El. The similar Methushelach — Methuselah, in the line of Seth — is a different name of a different man, though the resemblance has caused confusion since antiquity.
biblical_def: Methusael is the fourth and last quiet name in the line of Cain before the narrative stops to describe his son. “Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech” (Gen 4:18). Everything Genesis has to say about the house is said through that son. Lamech is the first polygamist in Scripture: “And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah” (Gen 4:19) — a plain departure from the creation ordinance that a man shall cleave unto his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. From those two wives came the three culture-founders: “Adah bare Jabal: he was the father of such as dwell in tents, and of such as have cattle” (Gen 4:20), Jubal the father of all such as handle the harp and organ (Gen 4:21), and “Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron” (Gen 4:22). And from the same house came the boast. Methusael's name, if it means man of God, sits in that setting with a heavy irony: four generations from a fratricide, in a family of real genius, a man is called of God, and his son sings about murder to his wives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Methusael; in sacred history he is the son of Mehujael and the father of Lamech, in the line of Cain.
webster_full: METHUSAEL, n. Man of God; a proper name in the fourth chapter of Genesis.
The son of Mehujael, and the fourth in descent from Cain.
He was the father of Lamech, who took unto him two wives.
He is not to be confounded with Methuselah, the son of Enoch in the line of Seth.
Of his own life the Scripture has recorded nothing.
scriptures: And unto Enoch was born Irad: and Irad begat Mehujael: and Mehujael begat Methusael: and Methusael begat Lamech.
And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.
And his brother's name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ.
If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold.
corruption_summary: Lamech's two wives are now often cited to argue that Scripture endorses a plurality of marriage forms. Genesis records polygamy first as a mark of the line of Cain and never once commends it; the creation ordinance is one man and one woman, and Christ says so.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument runs that since the Bible narrates polygamy without an explicit prohibition in Genesis, marriage in Scripture is culturally variable and the modern insistence on one man and one woman is a later imposition. The text will not support it. The first polygamist named in the Bible is Lamech, the son of Methusael, in the line of Cain, and he is introduced in the same breath as his song about killing a man. Every subsequent instance in Scripture — Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon — is narrated with its griefs attached: rivalry, contempt, exile, and in Solomon's case the loss of the kingdom to idolatry. Narration is not approval, and the Bible is not a book that only condemns in the imperative mood.

The standard is fixed at the creation and reasserted by Christ against every relaxation: “Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female” (Mat 19:4), and therefore “they twain shall be one flesh” (Mat 19:5) — two, not three, and a bond He calls unbreakable by man. Paul requires an elder to be the husband of one wife. The dictionary's position is the plain one: marriage is one man and one woman covenanting before God for life, and the household of Methusael's son is Genesis showing the reader the first departure from it, in the same chapter as the first murder.
